To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the value creation capability of intellectual capital is contingent upon the interrelationships among its human, organisational, and social capital components and the type of HRSS services offered.

intellectual capital configurations, consisting of human, organizational and/or social capital, are value creation mechanisms for HRSS and the value creation capability of these configurations is dependent on the type of HRSS service.
Intellectual capital (IC) is a value driver of Human Resource Shared Service (HRSS) value creation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the value creating capabilities of HRSS and how they are able to create value for end users.
understanding the value creating capabilities of HRSS through the use of their IC.
how intellectual capital is configured to create value for HRSS, and the implications of these findings for the management of HRSS.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the value creation capability of HRSS is dependent on the type of HR service offered, which in turn depends on the IC configurations that are formed.
the interrelationships and interactions among human, organisaztional and social capital are critical in driving value creation for HRSS.
HRSS can create value through their IC configurations, which is contingent upon the HRSS type and the HR services offered.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the IC configuration approach provides a better understanding on the ways in which HRSS can leverage on their intellectual capital to create value.
intellectual capital is a key resource that can drive value creation for HRSS.

the value creation capability of HRSS is contingent on the type of services offered, and that the interrelationships and configurations of the three types of intellectual capital are key to value creation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the value creating potential of HRSS intellectual capital is not limited to its individual components but rather in the configurations that these form.

HRSS should not treat human, organisational, and social capital as independent and separate entities, but rather, they should be considered as a whole in order to understand how these three types of intellectual capital can be configured and how such configurations drive value creation.
the value of IC is not in the components themselves but in the configuration of the components that creates value for the end user.
